newsitem.title: USA: Cutting copper costs best course - Freeport.
newsitem.headline: Cutting copper costs best course - Freeport.

text.p: Cutting costs is the best course for steering through the uncertainty that still muddies copper's outlook months after Sumitomo stunned the red metal market with its revelations, said Richard Adkerson, chief financial officer of Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc.

"Our strategy is to protect our cost situation from the ups and downs the market will go through in the context of a good long-term business to be in," Adkerson told Reuters. "We will be profitable in any forseeable copper price environment."

Even though New Orleans-based Freeport, whose production operations are in Indonesia, had net cash copper production costs of less than 15 cents a lb in the second quarter, Adkerson felt there was no room for complacency.

But following the post-Sumitomo tumble in copper prices, Freeport's low production costs did allow it to dump all of its put options which protected floor prices up to June 1997, and cream off an extra $100 million in cash for its bottom line.
The put options, which caused financial grief for some banks who sold them to producers, originally cost Freeport 2 cents a lb to buy, and were cashed in at 8 cents per lb.
ASARCO and Phelps Dodge Corp took a similar path though stopped short of being completely unprotected.
Freeport now has no price protection on any production.

"Ultimately we are going to have to live with prices, and our hedge is our low cost position," Adkerson said. "If we could buy protection at levels we consider appropriate at reasonable cost, then we would consider it."
He escewed forecasting copper supply, demand or prices, and insisted the best policy is to focus on keeping costs low and looking for ways to reduce them further.

Some in the market would probably agree, especially after relying on dubious industry-wide market data over the past few years, prices which many believed were artificially high, and talk of unquantified stocks stashed away from exchange eyes.
And the large amounts of cheaper solvent extraction eletrowon (SX/EW) copper coming on stream will push down the average industry cash costs, leaving higher cost producers feeling vulnerable.

BHP Copper is scrambling to slash up to 10 cents a lb off production costs at its troubled Magma operations in the U.S., acquired at the start of the year. Magma's costs shot to 85 cents a lb - barely below Thursday's COMEX prices.
This year Freeport will produce 1.1 billion lbs of copper or just under 500,000 tonnes, and 1.6 million ounces of gold.

In 1998, output at the Indonesian mill will rise from the current 125,000 tonnes per day of ore to 190,000 to 200,000 tonnes a day. The amount of extra copper generated will depend on ore grades. RTZ Corp Plc has a stake in part of the expansion.

Adkerson said Freeport will continue to have surpluses in concentrates, but with expansion at the company's renamed Atlantic Copper (formerly RTM) in Huelva, Spain reaching maximum output of 270,000 tonnes on an annual basis in the second quarter this year, the suplus was manageable.
